title: COAP 2009 best paper award
contribution: The awardees' retrospective on 2002-2007: cross-field SDP x IP collaboration, loose augmented-Lagrangian/BCD SDP solving, the pivot from 0-1 IPs to nonconvex QP, and one of the first SDP-based B&B to beat an LP-based one (BoxQP).
problem_entry: Each author wanted to learn the other's field; SDP relaxations for 0-1 IPs were strong in theory but too large to compute (p. 1); later they searched for a class where SDP bounds win uniformly and quickly (p. 2).
key_idea: Augmented Lagrangian + block coordinate descent with loosely solved subproblems (pp. 1-2); then a finite KKT/complementarity B&B with LP+SDP relaxations made bounded by combining both (p. 2), tailored to box-constrained QP (p. 3).
assumptions: Nonconvex QP with linear constraints; COAP paper restricted to box constraints, up to 100 variables (pp. 2-3); no formal assumptions in the note.
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs); structural devices named: KKT reformulation as an LP with complementarity constraints for finite branching (p. 2)
combining LP and SDP relaxation features to make unbounded relaxations bounded (p. 2)
experiments: Summarized only: loose BCD still gave best-known QAPLIB bounds (p. 2); SDP B&B far outperformed LP branch-and-cut on BoxQP up to n = 100 (p. 3); no tables.
positioning: Credits Monteiro's first-order SDP survey (p. 1); hedged priority claim 'one of the first clear examples' of SDP B&B beating LP B&B; lists later adopters of AL+BCD and BoxQP becoming a standard MINLP test case (p. 3).
writing: Narrative arc motivation -> obstacle -> pivot ('So the authors shifted their focus away from IPs', p. 2) -> general moral (p. 3); unsigned third-person note that slips into first person in the Axioma paragraph (p. 3).
limits_future: Lessons: practical power of SDP for continuous nonconvex problems, paying for strong expensive relaxations, classic AL/BCD still matter (p. 3); no limits or future directions beyond the follow-on list.

method_links.note: loose inner solves discovered experimentally; origin story of H7

strong-but-expensive relaxation credo; object is an SDP+LP relaxation in finite B&B, not an exact reformulation

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Look for the class where the strong relaxation wins uniformly

transferable: When a strong relaxation is slow on one class, search for the class where it gives uniformly good bounds quickly and move there (p. 2).
For finite B&B on continuous nonconvex QP, reformulate via KKT as an LP with complementarity constraints and branch on complementarity (p. 2).
In augmented-Lagrangian SDP solvers, try only one or a few BCD cycles per outer iteration before solving subproblems accurately (p. 2).
coauthors: Dieter Vandenbussche (note unsigned; batch list names Burer and Vandenbussche)

quotes.text: Somewhat surprisingly, computational experiments showed that the dual multipliers converged reasonably well even when the subproblems were solved very loosely by only a few cycles of block coordinate descent.
More generally, the paper also illustrates that it can be worthwhile to pay for a computationally expensive, but strong, relaxation

title: Computable representations for convex hulls of low-dimensional quadratic forms
contribution: Exact computable representations of conv{[1 x; x xx^T]}: DNN for the simplex with n <= 4, PSD and RLT for the box with n = 2 (with a counterexample at n = 3), and a disjunctive representation for triangulated polytopes with n <= 3. Exploratory cuts for the 3-cube are certified numerically to be insufficient.
problem_entry: Representing C = conv{[1 x; x xx^T] : x in F} is fundamental for BARON-type relaxations of products; F is a simplex or box arising from partitioning, so study the two common choices in low dimension (p. 3).
key_idea: Read completely-positive matrix theory as hull theorems: DNN = CP for n <= 4 plus rank-one extreme points gives the simplex result (pp. 4-5); bordered transform Y+ = TYT^T plus the 2009 CP representation gives the box n = 2 result (pp. 6-7); triangulation gives a disjunctive representation for n <= 3 (p. 9).
assumptions: F a simplex, box/hyper-rectangle (affine map, general RLT), or triangulated polytope in low dimension; dimension limits are sharp (counterexamples n > 4 simplex, n = 3 box) (pp. 5, 8); parallelepiped omitted as rare in practice (p. 8).
proof_devices: extreme-point argument: DNN extreme points are CP by the Kogan-Berman graph criterion, then rank one by Bomze et al.; compactness (Theorem 1, p. 5)
slack lifting Y+ = TYT^T turning PSD and RLT into DNN, then an explicit CP factor with column rescaling lambda_i = (1/2)e^T(x^i + s^i) (Theorem 2, pp. 6-7)
explicit counterexample Q = (1/3)ee^T - I at n = 3: true -2/3 vs relaxation -3/4 (p. 8), found by inspecting the triangulation pieces (p. 10)
cut propagation by complementation symmetry: 8 maps give 4 distinct cuts (p. 10)
slice-and-plot at x = diag(X) = e/2 with 3-D projection; vertices in C and facets = cuts (pp. 10-11)
numerical non-membership certificate via the disjunctive formulation (p. 11)
experiments: Exploratory: random n = 3 instances almost always exact under PSD and RLT; 15 n = 30 instances (cited from Anstreicher): max gap 3.06%, average 0.41%, 0.00% on 8 (p. 9); numerically computed Fig. 1 with a caution (p. 11).
positioning: Generalizes and simplifies Linderoth's triangle result and extends the Al-Khayyal-Falk RLT box fact (p. 3); balanced comparison with Jach-Michaels-Weismantel explicit envelopes (p. 8); admits the simplex result is a straightforward consequence of existing CP theory (p. 3).
writing: Introduction announces each negative result next to the positive one (p. 3); exploratory part labelled as such (p. 9); prefers the simpler proof that is closer to the simplex case (p. 7); 11 printed pages.
limits_future: Cuts for the 3-cube do not give C; full characterization without extra variables is an open problem (pp. 9, 11-12).

method_links.note: small recurring substructures (simplex n <= 4, box n = 2); best relaxation shown exact at n = 2 and failing at n = 3 by counterexample; disjunctive form used as a certification device while a direct description is sought; boundary published as an open problem
the 2009 CP representation is the engine of the box proof; hulls read off from CP/DNN cone properties
computation proposes (random n = 3, triangulation inspection) but non-membership is certified only numerically, not in exact arithmetic

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Reuse your own exact representation as a lemma for small hulls
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the 2009 CP theorem (Prop. 3) is the proof device for the n = 2 box hull; recurs in S016 Theorem 2.4

transferable: Test whether a relaxation equals a hull by building an exact disjunctive representation (triangulation into simplices, each DNN-representable) and optimizing or checking membership over it (pp. 9, 11).
Find separating objectives by inspecting the pieces of the disjunction, then propagate cuts through the set's symmetry maps (complementation) and keep the distinct images (p. 10).
Visualize a hull gap by fixing the worst x and diag(X) and plotting the remaining three entries in 3-D; then verify vertices in C and facets equal the cuts (pp. 10-11).
Use the bordered transform Y+ = TYT^T, T = [1 0; 0 I; e -I], to turn PSD and RLT into a DNN condition so CP/DNN theorems apply to box problems (p. 6).

quotes.text: This result is a straightforward consequence of existing theory for completely positive matrices, but to our knowledge does not appear in the literature.
While we have not been able to answer this question fully, we now describe some exploratory results.

title: Optimizing a polyhedral-semidefinite relaxation of completely positive programs
contribution: An augmented-Lagrangian decomposition for the DNN relaxation of completely positive programs. It provides a valid lower bound at any time and, inside B&B, is about 10x faster than his own earlier Burer-Vandenbussche method on BoxQP, which made it the state of the art for global BoxQP at the time.
problem_entry: The 2009 CP representation of NQP gives a DNN relaxation that is polynomial but slow with IPMs: SeDuMi 1, 30, 385, 1787 s for n = 25-100, from O(n^2 x n^2) Newton systems (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Split DNN constraints into {Ax = b, diag(AXA^T) = b^2, Y psd}, moved into the cone J = {Z psd : MZM^T = 0} = N PSD N^T, and {binary/complementarity, Y >= 0, Y <= U}; AL on Y = Z with one BCD loop; closed-form projections and an any-time Lagrangian bound (pp. 4-10).
assumptions: Standard form Ax = b, x >= 0 (critical); known possibly infinite upper bounds x <= u giving Y <= U; finite bounds guarantee finite lower bounds (pp. 3, 5, 10).
proof_devices: Gram-factor argument MYM^T = 0 => MY = 0 via ||MV||_F^2 = 0 (Prop. 1, p. 6)
null-space parametrization J = {NPN^T : P psd} (Lemma 1, p. 7)
projection proj_J(R) = N proj_psd(N^T R N) N^T by completing the square; dual-cone projection via Moreau (Prop. 2, pp. 7-8); O(n^2 k) cost (p. 8)
valid bound from Lagrangian relaxation with S in J* so the Z-part vanishes (pp. 9-10)
no overall convergence proof; sigma rules experimental (pp. 11, 16)
experiments: Matlab+C/MEX, single thread (p. 11). Run time is defined as the time to reach the common bound v-hat (p. 12). 99 BoxQP instances (54+36+9 new): 10.21x faster on average, about 7x per iteration (pp. 12-13). 92 QAPLIB instances: 4.83x vs BV and 2.94x vs ZST; best known bound on tai35b; advantage shrinks with p (pp. 14-15). Replicated BV B&B tree with only the node solver swapped: 11.28x, and 20.50x at p = 125 (pp. 16-17). Quadratic multiple knapsack, 50 instances per cell: not competitive with specialized single-knapsack codes (pp. 18-19).
positioning: Continues his own AL-decomposition line begun with [7] (p. 4); baselines are his previous method and Zhao-Sun-Toh, with shared code (pp. 4, 19); state of the art for BoxQP by transitivity via VN branch-and-cut over BARON (p. 17); credits de Klerk-Sotirov and ZST where they win (pp. 14-15).
writing: Numbered main conclusions in the introduction (p. 5); caution that the summary of [7] is simplified (p. 10); hedged 'we believe, but have not rigorously proved' (pp. 13-14); candid 'Despite many attempts' about sigma0 (p. 12); each tuning rule given with its reason (p. 16).
limits_future: Sensitivity to sigma0 with per-class calibration (p. 12); shared O(p^6) PSD projection bottleneck (p. 15); loses to specialized knapsack methods (p. 18); future: general DNN conic programs, deciding which constraints go to the Y vs Z subproblem (p. 19).

transferable: Before designing a first-order method, time an IPM on a ladder of sizes and name the operation that blows up (p. 4).
Square linear equalities into the cone (MYM^T = 0 iff MY = 0 for psd Y) so that the constrained PSD face projects via one small eigendecomposition N proj(N^T R N) N^T (pp. 6-8).
Keep a valid lower bound at every outer iteration with a dual-feasible multiplier so an inexact SDP solver can be used inside B&B (pp. 9-10).
Compare bounding algorithms by time to the common bound v-hat on log-log scatter plots with y = x and y = 10x lines; decompose speed-up into per-iteration cost and iteration count (pp. 12-13).

To compare relaxation solvers inside B&B, freeze the incumbent code's tree logic and swap only the solver; warm-start children from parent multipliers and damp the penalty with sigma0 = sqrt(sigma) (p. 16).
Give a baseline without valid bounds a rigorous-bound post-processor (Jansson et al.) and report its overhead (p. 15).

quotes.text: Consistent with the experience of Burer–Vandenbussche [7] and other augmented-Lagrangian methods for SDP, we find that it pays only to solve these problems very loosely.
Though our method was successful for p ≈ 50, it was not competitive with the specialized method of [20].

title: The MILP road to MIQCP
contribution: A survey that reads MIQCP as the next step after MILP. It catalogs strong lifted relaxations (RLT, rank-2 linear and SOC products, PSD) and the cases where they give the hull, proves two new exactness theorems (orthant n <= 3; bounded quadratic form up to recession), reviews eigenvector-based disjunctive and projected cuts, and adds a BoxQP solver case study. Read in the preprint version.
problem_entry: Track MILP's influence on MIQCP to catalog results for MILP-trained readers and to set a road map; MIQCP as a progression from MILP, not a special case of MINLP; focus on relaxations, not global optimization (preprint pp. 1-2).
key_idea: All nonconvexity sits in X = xx^T in the lifted space, and optimization reduces to clconv F-hat (pp. 4-5). Static chain clconv F-hat within L, RLT, R2, S2 and PSD (Prop. 2.3, p. 7), with a catalog of exact cases (pp. 7-12). Dynamic cuts from univariate constraints along eigenvectors of X-hat - x-hat x-hat^T via a secant-split disjunction and CGLP, analogous to split cuts (pp. 18-20, 30). Projected x-space relaxations (pp. 26-27).
assumptions: MIQCP with possibly infinite bounds and integer bounds for integer variables (p. 2); LQ/CQ/NQ partition (p. 3); CPP theorem needs only boundedness of binary/complementarity variables (p. 16); sequential convexification needs bounded F, no integers (p. 17).
proof_devices: products of valid inequalities linearized: RLT, rank-2 linear, new rank-2 SOC x linear (S2) with worked example (preprint pp. 5-6)
recession-cone decomposition with CP factorization (DNN = CP for size <= 4), split by zeta_j > 0 (Lemma 2.2, preprint p. 9)
separating-hyperplane contradiction via a negative recession direction from a CP factor column (Theorem 2.4, preprint p. 10)
Pataki rank bound with case analysis on finiteness of b_l, b_u forcing rank-one extreme points (Theorem 2.7, preprint pp. 11-12)
binary shift identity (x_i - l_i)^2 = x_i - l_i linearized (Prop. 2.4, preprint p. 8)
worked CGLP disjunctive cut on GLOBALLib st_ph11 showing that bound convexification alone cannot cut the point (preprint pp. 20-22)
experiments: Reproduced Saxena et al. study on 129 GLOBALLib instances, filtered to vRLT > v*, measured as % gap closed relative to RLT, with ablations V1/V2/V2-SI/V2-Dsj: 24.80/76.49/44.40/41.54% (preprint pp. 23-24); eigenvalue trajectories on 3 instances picked by stated criteria (p. 25). New case study on 9 spar100 BoxQP instances: ipm 5,355-10,296 s vs cp 54-101 s vs proj 538-1,510 s preprocessing + about 1-2 s solve; gap closed cp 98-99% vs proj 92-96% (pp. 28-29).
positioning: MILP lineage (Dantzig et al., Padberg, Balas sequential convexification, lift-and-project) with a closing MILP-vs-MIQCP concept table (preprint pp. 1, 16-17, 30); acknowledges Belotti's general MINLP disjunctive cuts (p. 3); own results listed as catalog entries among others' (pp. 7, 14-16).
writing: Two-fold aims sentence: catalog plus roadmap (p. 1); new results flagged 'As far as we are aware' (pp. 9, 11); numbered remarks on computations (pp. 23-24, 28-29); ends with a comparative table (p. 30).
limits_future: Relaxations solved by IPMs lack reoptimization, a B&B bottleneck; exact descriptions unknown beyond very small cases (preprint p. 30); propose LP outer approximations of convex quadratic cuts for warm starts (p. 29); open: recession-cone relationship (p. 12); breakthroughs yet to come (p. 1).

method_links.note: catalog by dimension and substructure (box n <= 2, orthant n <= 3, simplex n <= 4); intersection L-RLT-R2-S2-PSD is an early explicit kitchen sink; S2 (SOC x linear) is a precursor of SOC-RLT
lifted view 'hard quadratic -> easy linear'; CPP exact hull (Theorem 3.3); CP-factor argument reused for a new hull theorem
instance filter vRLT > v* disclosed with count; illustrative instances chosen by stated criteria (reported Saxena et al. study)
specialized vs black-box solver comparison used as a survey-level argument, not a same-day prototype

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: closing Table 6 maps each MILP concept (relaxation, exact description, elementary and transformed nonconvexity, sequential convexification) to its MIQCP analogue; direct case of H2

transferable: Generate lifted valid inequalities by multiplying every pair of valid constraints (including linear x SOC) and linearizing; name families by source and test each family's contribution to the hull (preprint pp. 5-7).
Prove exactness on unbounded sets by showing relaxation = conv F-hat + recession cone and arguing by contradiction through a negative recession direction (preprint pp. 9-10).
For PSD systems with p equalities and q inequalities, use Pataki's rank bound case by case to force rank-one extreme points (preprint pp. 11-12).
Ablate a cut family three ways: new cuts, cheap surrogate cuts on the same nonconvexities, and new cuts on a weaker base relaxation (preprint pp. 23-24).
Give a 3-variable worked example where even full convexification with respect to bounds fails to cut off the point, to motivate stronger machinery (preprint pp. 21-22).

quotes.text: the “breakthrough” results are yet to come and we believe that the past of MILP holds the clues to the future of MIQCP.
In this sense, we view (MIQCP) as a natural progression from MILP rather than, say, a special case of MINLP.

title: Non-convex mixed-integer nonlinear programming: A survey
contribution: A survey of non-convex MINLP that moves from key ingredients (estimators, separability, factorization, spatial branching) to algorithms, then a detailed treatment of the quadratic case and software. It closes by advocating MINLP-specific convex-hull analysis, special-case algorithms and heuristics.
problem_entry: For non-convex MINLP even the continuous relaxation is a global optimization problem; small instances can defeat existing methods; existing surveys cover the convex case, so this one focuses on the non-convex and quadratic cases (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Organize by ingredients, then algorithms, then the quadratic case, then software, giving each concept one concrete example (McCormick, alphaBB under-estimator, factorization of exp(sqrt(y1y2+y3)), spatial branching on z = y^2) (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: General MINLP form (p. 2); bounded feasible regions in practice (p. 3); polynomials reducible to quadratics with possible overhead (pp. 3, 6).
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs); expository devices: one worked example and figure per concept (pp. 3-5)
positioning: Credits chemical engineering for early MINLP work (p. 3); branch-and-reduce 'a major step forward' (p. 5); balanced view of alphaBB (p. 5); notes the PLF infeasibility pitfall (p. 6); lists five global solvers (p. 8); self-citation confined to the quadratic sections (pp. 7-8).
writing: Table of contents plus structure paragraph (pp. 2-3); short attributed paragraphs; first-person advocacy in conclusions ('We believe', 'We also advocate') (pp. 8-9).
limits_future: Expository, no new results; future: convex hulls needing polyhedral theory plus convex analysis, special-case algorithms as incubators of new techniques, heuristics and approximation algorithms (pp. 8-9).

method_links.note: stated program: analyze and cut convex hulls arising in MINLPs using polyhedral theory and convex analysis
CP rather than PSD lifted matrix for x >= 0 yields stronger relaxations (brief, stated)

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: advocates algorithms for special cases because they allow new techniques (SDP) that later generalize; same stance in S016 road map and S010's restriction to common F

transferable: Survey structure: key concepts each with one worked example and figure, then algorithms built from them, then your special case, then software, then explicit 'we believe/we advocate' directions (pp. 2-9).
Explain spatial branching with a one-variable picture of z = y^2 relaxed on [0, u] before and after splitting, in both the convex and LP versions (pp. 4-5).

quotes.text: Special cases can also allow the development of newer techniques (e.g., semidefinite relaxations), which may then progress to more general techniques.

For example, analyzing — and generating cutting planes for — the various convex hulls that arise in MINLPs (see Section 5.4) will require aspects of both polyhedral theory and convex analysis to achieve best results.
